newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil has new Sao Paulo sugar/alcohol group.
newsitem.headline: Brazil has new Sao Paulo sugar/alcohol group.

text.p: Brazilian sugar and alcohol producers in the key producing state of Sao Paulo have joined to form one new organisation - the Sao Paulo Sugar Industry Union, or Unica, the union's president said.
Unica unites 121, or 90.98 percent, of Sao Paulo's 133 sugar and alcohol production units, said Sergio Simoes Ometto, also president of the Da Barra factory, the largest in the world.
"Many voices were saying many different things to the government. And so we decided we needed one voice," Ometto said.
With sugar output of 7.85 million tonnes, its members will account for 98.44 percent of production in Sao Paulo and 57.72 percent of all Brazilian output.
Its alcohol production seen at 8.53 million cubic meters represents 95.08 percent of the state's production and 59.87 percent of the country's total alcohol output.

Previously the largest representative body in the region had been the Sao Paulo Sugar and Alcohol Industries Association (AIAA) whose members had accounted for 68.2 percent of sugar and 53.2 percent of alcohol production in the state.
The AIAA will now cease to exist but for the time being Unica will use its former headquarters as its base.
The idea for the union came when producers were discussing the 1997/98 sugar crop plan with the government, Ometto said.

Sao Paulo producers throughout the talks fought to have free exports, not because they felt total shipments will be higher than the 5.39 million tonnes eventually set out in the plan, but because they objected to individual export quotas per factory.

They refused to submit a breakdown by factory for sugar exports from the region whereupon the government published its crop plan on April 30 with its own calculations for the state and laying great emphasis nationally on alcohol production.
"We think they put too much alcohol, we do not need to produce so much alcohol. We do not accept the numbers they gave, we do not accept the export quota," Ometto said.
Producers are still waiting for a further decree to be published which will allow exports set out within the crop plan to go ahead with a zero export tax.
This, according to Mauricio Assis, head of the Industry and Commerce Ministry's primary commodities department, was being drawn up and should be published this week.
Ometto was confident within the next few months government officials would also reduce to zero the export tax on any sugars available above the export quota.
"The zero tax will only be for the excess sugars set out in the crop plan," he said.
